# BDH-CQ: In-Context Learning with Recurrent Latent Reasoning

- **Authors**: Björn Engdahl, Adrian Kosowski, Jan Chorowski, Zuzanna Stamirowska, Przemysław Uznański, Junlin Jiang, Rohan Phadke, Remigiusz Kinas, Richard Zhong
- **Venue**: cs.NE
- **Published**: 2026-08-10
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09888>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.09888v1>
- **Topics**: reasoning-faithfulness
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-evaluation 0.25, reasoning-faithfulness 0.50, reasoning-training 0.25

## In one line

Combines in-context learning through evolving recurrent memory with iterative reasoning in a continuous latent workspace that is never decoded into language, reaching 29.5% pass@2 on public ARC-AGI-1 at $0.0007 per task from 150M parameters, and then probes with controlled tasks what the resulting demonstration-bound operators can and cannot do.

## Problem

Chain-of-thought couples reasoning to serial narration: every intermediate state must be projected through a discrete vocabulary, emitted autoregressively and consumed again before computation can continue, and as traces have grown so have tokens, latency and cost. Latent reasoning removes that constraint but has developed separately from in-context learning. Reasoning language models learn flexibly from context yet allocate extra computation through generated tokens; compact recursive solvers reason iteratively in latent space but their ARC pipelines are transductive, optimising on augmented demonstration pairs from the evaluation tasks themselves with a learned identity embedding per puzzle, so an unseen task requires a backward pass before it can be attempted. Nothing acquires an unseen transformation from demonstrations alone, at inference, in latent space.

## Contributions

- BDH-CQ: in-context learning through evolving recurrent memory combined with iterative reasoning in a structured continuous latent space, where demonstrations of an unseen task write to memory at inference and no parameters are updated -- in contrast to recursive ARC solvers that require backward-pass adaptation and a learned identity embedding per puzzle.
- A new point on the ARC-AGI-1 cost-accuracy frontier: 29.5% pass@2 at a computed $0.00070 per task from 150M parameters, roughly three orders of magnitude below the per-task cost reported for task-trained recursive solvers.
- A separation of consistent rule application from isolated correct outputs, using strict task accuracy against test-pair accuracy, which surfaces 52 of 160 ConceptARC tasks with one or two correct test inputs and no consistent rule.
- Controlled post-freeze probes with deterministic oracles that vary one factor at a time and extend beyond the demonstrated range, showing that propagation and copying extrapolate without a ceiling while ordering and nesting fail at characteristic depths with opposite error signatures.
- A context intervention on byte-identical inputs that distinguishes failure to extrapolate from failure to execute: matched support fully repairs the nesting cliff and only partly repairs long ordering.
- An opaque-identifier, concept-mixed replication ruling out request-side cues as an explanation of the ConceptARC score, reported with an explicit statement of what it does not rule out.

## Method

Demonstrations presented at inference continuously update a recurrent memory; the query is then solved by iterative computation in a structured high-dimensional latent workspace, with only the answer decoded and no intermediate state expressed in language. No task identifiers or evaluation-task demonstration pairs enter training and no parameters are updated at inference. ARC is used as both benchmark and experimental substrate because it specifies new visual transformations through sparse demonstrations and demands exact outputs, which makes rule consistency directly inspectable; the authors call the resulting behaviour a demonstration-conditioned operator schema and design controlled probes for what it binds, how far it extrapolates, what it composes with and where execution fails. Those probes are generated after the model is frozen, with deterministic oracles producing every target output, three demonstrations and two held-out inputs per task, and one factor varied at a time -- propagation distance, number of motif copies, sequence length to be ordered, and depth of nested containment -- with held-out instances deliberately beyond the demonstrated range. A context intervention re-runs byte-identical hard inputs under a short context that stops below the test complexity and a supported context that adds one demonstration at the target complexity, which separates failure to extrapolate from failure to execute. A composition probe holds canvas, source, anchor and semantics fixed across three dense motif families and compares each operation alone against its composition with relocation. A confound replication resends the same grids with cryptographically opaque identifiers in concept-mixed batches. Strict task accuracy -- all three test inputs of a task correct -- is the primary measure, reported alongside test-pair accuracy so that consistent rule application is distinguishable from success on individual inputs.

## Results

On the 400-task public ARC-AGI-1 evaluation, a 150M-parameter configuration reaches 24.25% pass@1 and 29.50% pass@2 (Wilson [25.24, 34.15]) at a computed $0.00070 per task, against ARC Prize's reported $1.48 and $1.76 per task for two task-trained recursive solvers -- roughly three orders of magnitude cheaper, which is the paper's claim to a new cost-accuracy frontier point rather than to a new accuracy. On ConceptARC it reaches 59.38% strict task pass@2 and 77.92% test-pair pass@2. That 18.5-point gap is the paper's most interesting internal result and it is analysed rather than glossed: under pass@2 the system solves zero test pairs for 13 tasks, one for 15, two for 37 and all three for 95, so 52 of 160 tasks have one or two correct test inputs without being solved -- under a rule-induction account a correctly induced rule should transfer to every test input, so partial success is direct evidence that the transformation is not being applied consistently. The controlled probes give sharply different generalisation profiles. Boundary propagation stays correct on 48/48 held-out outputs across distances 2 to 8 and copying on 48/48 as target sites rise from one to four, neither reaching a ceiling. Ordering is nearly saturated through five objects then collapses to 29/36 at six, 8/24 at seven and 1/24 at eight; nesting is saturated through depth four and falls to 29/36 at five. The two failures have opposite signatures: at ordering length eight only 3/24 outputs even have the right dimensions, whereas all 36 depth-five nesting outputs have correct dimensions with mean best-candidate cell accuracy above 99.9%, typically differing by a single containment decision. The context intervention then separates the causes: supplying one demonstration at the target complexity raises depth-five nesting from 19/24 to 24/24, so the nesting cliff is largely a failure to extrapolate demonstrated relation depth, while length-eight ordering recovers only 13/24 from 0/24 and therefore retains a genuine execution bottleneck. Composition is operation-dependent rather than uniform: relocation, reflection and rotation each solve 72/72 alone, rotation composed with relocation stays at 72/72, reflection composed with relocation drops to 47/72, and colour swap manages 26/72 alone and 0/72 composed -- though the authors note the two shuffled families reach only 1/24 in isolation, so the composed failure cannot be attributed to composition alone. Dense contextual binding is strong: a fresh colour permutation defined by demonstrations is applied correctly to all 96 held-out outputs at rank one. The confound replication moves nothing (374/480 pairs in both conditions, 96 against 95 tasks, with exactly six semantic-only and six opaque-only successes), though only 276/480 complete candidate lists agree across the two runs, so request context or search path changes the outputs without changing the score. Increasing latent reasoning effort raises accuracy monotonically (21% at low, 27% at medium, 29.5% at high, at 22% and 11% cost reductions), while a minimum-effort setting on the full evaluation costs a third as much for 111/400 against 118/400 -- a comparison the authors report as statistically unresolved (two-sided exact McNemar p = 0.167). Repeated identical requests were byte-identical at both effort tiers.

## Limitations

Stated, and unusually carefully. The ConceptARC replication rules out a combined identifier-and-batch confound but explicitly does not make ConceptARC a fresh benchmark, does not rule out exposure through training or checkpoint selection, and does not isolate the two interventions factorially. Ten tasks per concept family is called a profile rather than a reliable ranking, with the Wilson intervals for 9/10 and 2/10 overlapping broadly. And nominal pass@2 should not be read as two independently sampled attempts, since all 75 single-candidate records in the opaque replication were already correct at rank one. Not stated but worth noticing: the headline is a cost-efficiency claim and the accuracy is 29.5% on a benchmark where far more expensive systems score much higher, so the Pareto framing is doing real work and the comparison to $1.48 and $1.76 per task is against systems whose cost includes puzzle-specific optimisation the authors' does not need -- an architecture difference as much as an efficiency one. The controlled probes are generated by the authors after freezing the model, which is the right protocol, but they are ARC-like synthetic families of their own construction, so the extrapolation and composition conclusions are about those constructions. Nothing here is tested outside visual grid transformations, and the paper's own closing section lists language and mathematical reasoning as future work.

## Why it matters here

- **reasoning-faithfulness**: A system with no trace at all is a useful boundary case for this topic, because it forces the question of what one would even ask of it. The paper's answer is behavioural and it is the transferable part: it separates producing a correct output from having induced a rule, by scoring strict task accuracy alongside test-pair accuracy and reporting that 52 of 160 tasks get one or two of three test inputs right without being solved. Under a rule-induction account, a correctly induced rule transfers to every input of its task, so partial success is evidence against the rule having been induced -- an 18.5-point consistency gap that a per-pair metric would have shown as 77.92% success. That is a faithfulness question asked without any trace to inspect, and it is cleaner than most trace-based versions of it, because the ground truth is exact and the consequence of an inconsistent rule is visible. The controlled probes do the same thing at finer grain, and the error signatures are what make them informative: ordering fails by producing outputs of the wrong dimensions, nesting fails with correct dimensions and better than 99.9% cell accuracy differing in one containment decision. Two different failures that a single accuracy number would have merged. The context intervention on byte-identical inputs then attributes them differently -- adding one demonstration at the target depth repairs nesting completely and long ordering only halfway -- which is the sort of controlled attribution the archive should want before accepting any claim about what a model 'cannot do'. Read against the archive's latent-reasoning material, this supports the position that monitorability is not simply lost when reasoning goes latent: what is lost is the trace, and what remains available is consistency across inputs of a task, extrapolation profiles, composition behaviour and error structure, all of which the authors measure. The caution to attach when citing it: the headline is cost efficiency at 29.5% accuracy, the probes are synthetic families of the authors' own construction, and nothing here leaves visual grid transformations.

## Abstract

We introduce BDH-CQ, a reasoning model that combines in-context learning with recurrent latent reasoning. Inputs presented at inference time continuously update the model's recurrent memory; the model then solves a query through iterative computation in a high-dimensional latent space, without verbalizing its intermediate reasoning. We evaluate the model on the public ARC-AGI-1 evaluation set and use controlled ARC-like interventions to study what it learns from demonstrations, how consistently it applies an inferred transformation, and which concepts remain difficult. A 150M-parameter configuration reaches 29.5% pass@2 at a computed inference cost of \$0.0007 per task. This operating point breaks through the previously reported ARC-AGI-1 cost-accuracy Pareto frontier, establishing a new state of the art in benchmark cost efficiency.
